event_info.event_description: Analyze for disclosures on global pandemic risks. Look for corporate language discussing widespread impacts like supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote work transitions, and fundamental shifts in consumer demand.

holistic_analysis: Bank of America’s 2023 filing makes clear that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a live, material driver of risk across the franchise.  Management acknowledges that COVID-19 has already produced measurable, adverse effects – from supply-chain bottlenecks and labour shortages to direct hits on earnings – and warns that the ultimate trajectory of the virus, variants and policy responses will dictate further impacts.  The narrative spans both realised losses (e.g., compliance costs tied to rapid deployment of relief programmes) and forward-looking threats, such as elevated credit losses in sectors like office real-estate and shifts in consumer demand that could permanently reshape the loan book.  Operationally, the bank highlights stresses created by widespread remote work and reliance on digital channels.  These disclosures are recent (within three years of the 2020 outbreak) and specific to BAC’s business lines, but they stop short of providing quantified dollar figures or precise probability assessments.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic therefore warrants moderate-to-high severity scoring (generally 5-9 points per sentence), reflecting that the event is ongoing, has already affected results and still poses significant uncertainty to capital, liquidity and earnings.

evidence_list.snippet: The COVID-19 pandemic has directly and indirectly negatively impacted the global economy, disrupted global supply chains, adversely affected equity market valuations, created significant volatility and disruption in financial and capital markets, resulted in challenging labor market conditions, and adversely impacted our financial results to varying degrees and in various respects.

components.reason: Links pandemic to broad, macro-level harms (‘directly and indirectly negatively impacted the global economy’).
Names multiple widespread impacts – supply chains, labour shortages, market volatility – signalling severity and breadth.
States realised adverse effect on BAC’s own financial results.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Explicit, comprehensive description of past, material impacts on both the macro economy and BAC’s earnings yields a high severity score.

evidence_list.snippet: Such evolving impacts of the pandemic could disrupt the U.S. and global economy, including changes in financial and capital markets, and adversely affect our businesses and operations, liquidity, results of operations and financial condition, including from increased allowance for credit losses and noninterest expenses, which are dependent on the pandemic’s duration and severity.

components.reason: Forward-looking disclosure that COVID-19 ‘could disrupt’ and ‘adversely affect’ core financial metrics signals ongoing risk.
Calls out specific financial channels (liquidity, credit-loss allowance, expenses).
Highlights uncertainty tied to pandemic’s duration/severity, underscoring potential volatility.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Sentence forecasts multiple material downside channels tied to pandemic evolution; specificity but no quantification keeps score in upper-mid range.

evidence_list.snippet: Certain sectors also remain at risk (e.g., commercial real estate office exposure, consumer discretionary industries) as a result of shifts in demand from the pandemic.

components.reason: Identifies concrete vulnerable sectors linked to pandemic demand shifts.
Uses ‘remain at risk’ – signalling persistence of threat.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Sector-specific, forward-looking risk acknowledgement is meaningful but narrower in scope, earning a moderate score.

evidence_list.snippet: We could also experience continued and long-term negative impacts to our commercial credit exposure and an increase in credit losses within those industries that may be permanently impacted by a change in consumer preferences resulting from COVID-19 (e.g., commercial real estate exposure) or other industry disruptions.

components.reason: Projects ‘continued and long-term’ negative impacts on credit exposure – emphasises duration.
Direct link between pandemic-driven consumer preference changes and higher credit losses.
Notes possibility of permanent structural shift, heightening strategic risk.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Long-term credit-loss risk tied to permanent demand changes pushes severity toward the higher end of medium range.

evidence_list.snippet: We have experienced increased operational, reputational and compliance risk as a result of the prior need to rapidly deploy and implement multiple and varying pandemic relief programs, including the processing of unemployment benefits for California and certain other states, which have resulted in and will continue to result in losses.

components.reason: Describes realised increase in operational/compliance risk from COVID-19 relief work.
Admits programme has ‘resulted in and will continue to result in losses’ – direct financial impact.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Concrete example of pandemic-driven losses in operations and compliance, but limited to a single activity, gives a solid but mid-tier score.
